title: Broker Fallback Hierarchy - Operator Guide
author: Priya Kapoor
body:
Overview

This operator guide documents the Broker Fallback Hierarchy used in Redwood Private VPC and on-prem installations. The hierarchy defines ordered fallback tiers (level0, level1, level2) and the operator-facing controls, observability checks, and safe rollout/rollback patterns required to maintain availability and quality during capacity or model-quality incidents.

Scope and audience
- Scope: tenant routing and fallback behavior inside the customer VPC or on-prem runtime. Includes routing policy fields, operational knobs, alerts, and runbooks.
- Audience: runtime-ops, infra-ops, SRE, solutions engineering, and field engineers supporting private deployments.

Architecture summary
- request-router: runtime component that applies tenant policies and selects execution targets. Default primary path is model-exec.
- fallback brokers: lightweight routers for each tier. Typical names are fallback-broker-l0, fallback-broker-l1, fallback-broker-l2.
- model-exec: GPU-backed worker pool (quantized variants allowed).
- kv-cache: shard-aware prefix cache used to reduce cost and latency for repeated prefixes.
- control-plane agent: enforces tenant-level routing policy artifacts and receives propagated updates.

Fallback tiers and capabilities
- level0: same-family model variants with equivalent quantization and fidelity. Expected best-quality.
- level1: lower-cost quantized variants or smaller-family models that are compatible for most tasks.
- level2: cache responder or CPU-based degraded execution used as last-resort.

Policy model (key fields)
- preferred_variants: ordered list of model identifiers to try before falling back.
- min_quality_score: task-specific threshold, expressed as a decimal (for example, 0.85).
- max_latency_ms: absolute upper limit for response latency.
- cost_ceiling_per_request_usd: maximum acceptable spend per request for the tenant.
- fallback_allowed: boolean flag to permit automated fallback.

Operator knobs (examples)
- request selection timeout: default 120 ms. If primary selection does not complete within this window, router evaluates fallback policy.
- per-tenant concurrency limit: protects model-exec from tenant storms.
- tier qps limits: per-tier caps to prevent fallback brokers from overwhelming downstream resources.
- escalation timeouts: time to wait before moving to the next fallback tier.

Recommended SLOs for private deployments
- Availability SLO: 99.95% of requests return successful responses that meet min_quality_score, measured over a 30-day window.
- Latency SLOs: p50 < 65 ms, p95 < 250 ms (level0); p95 < 500 ms (level1); p95 < 2000 ms (level2).
- Fallback budget: level2 traffic should not exceed 3% of total monthly traffic without explicit approval.

Runbook: automatic fallback after GPU preemption
1) Detection: telemetry shows a sustained increase in model-exec errors or a cloud provider preemption alert.
2) Automatic router behavior: mark affected model-exec pool unhealthy and route new requests to fallback-broker-l0.
3) Immediate operator actions (within first 10 minutes): verify provider preemption, check fallback-broker-l0 capacity, and confirm policy propagation to agent. If fallback traffic exceeds 20% sustained for 10 minutes, open incident PRV-BROKER-ESCALATE.
4) Mitigation steps: provision short-term GPU capacity if available, temporarily relax tier qps limits if safe, notify customers if SLA may be affected.
5) Recovery: slowly ramp traffic back to model-exec when pool health returns to at least 90% of baseline. Use a 5-minute linear ramp by the request-router.

Runbook: operator-requested temporary cost window
1) Customer requests reduced per-request spend for a limited period.
2) Steps: update tenant policy via control-plane agent with a new cost_ceiling_per_request_usd and set preferred_variants accordingly. Propagate policy and validate via the agent propagation endpoint.
3) Monitor quality metrics for 15 minutes. If quality regresses beyond customer-approved threshold, revert policy. Record action in the policy history.

Upgrade and rollback guidance
- Canary pattern: apply changes to fallback brokers in a single AZ and shift a small percentage of traffic (<2%) for 30-60 minutes while observing p95 latency and error rates.
- Progressive rollout: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% with watch windows between stages. Abort if p95 increases by more than 30% absolute or error rate increases by > 1% for critical tenants.
- Rollback: routing is separated from execution. To rollback, re-point request-router selectors to the previous broker version and confirm metrics normalize. Persist policy snapshots before any change.

Testing and validation checklist
- Unit tests for policy parsing and decision logic.
- Integration tests: simulate full model pool outage, partial eviction, cold cache, and degraded variant throttling.
- Chaos tests: orchestrate simulated preemptions and assert combined level0+level1 availability >= 99.5% in the test window.
- Quality validation: run a representative prompt set across tiers and produce a regression report before enabling automated fallback for regulated customers.

Minimal observability to deploy
- Dashboard: Fallback traffic by tier with p50/p95 latency and QPS.
- Dashboard: Escalation events with counts and root-reasons.
- Alert: P0 if system-wide level2 traffic > 5% sustained for 15 minutes.
- Alert: P1 if single-tenant level1 fallback > 30% sustained for 30 minutes.

Onboarding checklist for customers
1) Confirm acceptable fallback tiers and quality thresholds in the onboarding questionnaire.
2) Execute a preflight simulation that triggers a small amount of fallback traffic and collect quality metrics.
3) Provide the customer a written fallback policy and escalation contacts.
4) Agree on fallback budget and notification cadence.

Example policy snippet (human readable)
- tenant_id: tenant-123
- preferred_variants: model-a-v2, model-a-v2-quant, model-a-cpu
- min_quality_score: 0.87
- max_latency_ms: 400
- cost_ceiling_per_request_usd: 0.0020
- fallback_allowed: true

Appendix: recommended resource sizing (per-tier, example)
- level0: GPU node, 8 CPU cores, 1 x A100, 64 GB RAM, expected p95 150-250 ms.
- level1: GPU node (quantized), 4 CPU cores, 1 x A10G, 48 GB RAM, expected p95 300-500 ms.
- level2: CPU responder or cache server, 8 CPU cores, no GPU, 32 GB RAM, expected p95 500-2000 ms.

Contacts and ownership
- runtime-ops: primary owner for request-router and fallback brokers.
- infra-ops: owner for GPU provisioning and cloud liaison.
- telemetry: owner for aggregators, dashboards, and alerts.
- customer-success: owner for customer communication templates and SLAs.
